title: Metadata tied to particular timestamps
statement: As a bioimage analyst,\nI want to save metadata tied to particular timestamps,\nso we can correctly process data acquired in non-uniform sampling protocols, used in e.g. long time lapses and smart microscopy setups.
workaround: RFC-5 coordinate transform mapping frames to acquisition time

title: Timestamps for non-uniform temporal sampling
statement: As an image analyst working with live-imaging data I encounter data that is non-uniformly sampled in time. This could be due to interruptions in long-term acquisitions or experimentally preferred variable sampling rates (e.g., lower sampling rate early on when a sample is more susceptible to photo-toxicity, event based changes to sampling rate in a smart microscopy setting). I want to store per-frame timestamps that allow correct visualization and processing (e.g., velocity estimation) of the data. The example stores POSIX timestamps as a parquet table, or as an array in the DCA metadata. In OME-Zarr v0.6 an alternative would be to use a RFC-5 coordinates transform.
workaround: RFC-5 coordinates (time array); else parquet table or custom attributes

title: Some channels only imaged at certain time points
statement: As a bioimage analyst in a microscopy core facility, I came across the following problem: I want to convert time lapse data generated by a high-content screening microscope to ome-zarr. The problem is that some channels are acquired at all time points, while other channels are only acquired at some time points. This is to reduce the amount of acquired data, as not all channels are needed for time-dependent analysis. The question is now how best to save this into ome-zarr. Should all channels be saved into one zarr-array with the missing time-points / channels as zeros? Or should the channels be saved in separate arrays and connected with appropriate transforms?

title: Some channels as z-stacks, others as single planes
statement: As a bioimage analyst in a microscopy core facility, I came across the following problem: I want to convert data generated by a high-content screening microscope to ome-zarr. The problem is that for some channels the entire z-stack is saved, while for other channels only a single 2D image is saved. They can either be a single z-slice, or a projected image. This is to reduce the amount of acquired data, as not all channels are needed for 3D analysis. The question is now how best to save this into ome-zarr. Should all channels be saved into one zarr-array with the missing z-slices / channels as zeros? Or should the channels be saved in separate arrays and connected with appropriate transforms? Usually the same metadata will apply to the 2D image as the z-stack. Is there a place to write this once and reference across the two zarr files? Is this solved by collections/RFC-8?

title: Per-timepoint normalization statistics and annotations
statement: As a data scientist, I may want to pre-compute and store summary statistics at the dataset level or per timepoint when processing images. This is helpful so that I (or other downstream users) can later apply different types of data normalization approaches efficiently without reading full images. It’s also possible there might be other timepoint annotations, such as timestamps or the timepoint of an ablation or intervention, that I want to save. There isn’t a convention for how to store these timepoint annotations or statistics in ome-zarr or other metadata that are indexed by timepoint. Where should these data be stored? If you have a lot of timepoints, this can make the zarr.json really large and overcrowd other metadata stored there. It could be saved in a tabular format as well or as an array. Also, how do we want to index time? Should we use frames or the origin timestamp + gap from the previous frame (relevant to the non-uniform temporal sampling story as well)? How does this impact downsampled arrays?

title: Biological annotations for channels
statement: As a data scientist, I would like to index and record the type of channel and relevant biology in a dataset. While most processing pipelines assume a fixed, ordered set of channels, this breaks down across a large repository of data. For some channel types (i.e. fluorescence), it’s helpful to include target, marker, labeled structures, labeled molecules, or marker type. For other channel types (i.e. label-free), simple free-text descriptions could work. How does the community want to reference and look up biological relevant annotations (i.e. by name or index)? What is the core model that’s relevant for all channels? In an HCS plate, this information may be duplicated many times within a zarr. Where is this information stored? Is there a way to only reference it once?
workaround: DCA channel-metadata spec

title: Linear intensity calibration
statement: As a bioimage analyst in a microscopy core facility,\nI want to have calibrated intensity values of my images. I would like to apply different corrections, like subtraction of a constant background value, and linear scaling of intensities. One example would be, that we want to compensate for varying instrument sensitivity over long periods of time. We can track the instrument performance with reference measurements and then correct the images accordingly. Burning these corrections into the data has several downsides, like duplication / alteration of data, or reduction in intensity resolution (when rounding floats to integers). Therefore, it would be great, if these intensity calibrations could be described in the spec somewhere.

title: Nonlinear intensity calibration
statement: As a bioimage analyst in a microscopy core facility,\nI want to have calibrated intensity values of my images. For example, a detector can have a non-linear response to the incoming light intensity, i.e. it is less efficient at high photon count rates. If I have a calibration curve of the detector, I can account for this. Burning these corrections into the data has several downsides, like duplication / alteration of data, or reduction in intensity resolution (when rounding floats to integers). Therefore, it would be great, if these intensity calibrations could be described in the spec somewhere.

title: Spatially varying intensity correction
statement: As a bioimage analyst in a microscopy core facility,\nI want to be able to account for inhomogeneous illumination. Microscopes often have inhomogeneous illumination across the field of view. One can account for this by dividing the image by a reference “flatfield” image. Burning these corrections into the data leads to duplication / alteration of the original data. Therefore, it would be great, if these corrections could be described in the spec somewhere.

title: Metadata at different collection levels
statement: Related to biological DCA metadata, I might want to write some components associated with a set of movies (e.g., generated in one acquisition all containing the same biological specimen) and others with only a subset of them (e.g., perturbation conditions within an experiment).

title: Per-coordinate transforms along c and t
statement:
As an image analyst and microscopy pipeline developer,
I want to be able to apply different transforms to different coordinates along a non-spatial image dimension of an existing image,
so that I can save the transformations resulting from processing steps such as the following in OME-Zarr transformation metadata, avoiding the need for resampling of the image data: drift correction (one transformation per coordinate along dim t); channel alignment (one transformation per coordinate along dim c).

Note: RFC5 mentions the by-coordinate transformation in "future possibilities".
workaround: Resample data; RFC-5 lists by-coordinate transforms as future possibility

title: Large-scale tile stitching
statement: As a method developer for stitching large scale tiles, I would want the following:\n1. extend the spec with additional transformation types, so that new registration methods (e.g. non-rigid or other models) can be represented without waiting for a core spec revision.\n2. alignment information to live separately from the image data, so that I can compare multiple alignment solutions and compare them.

title: Images with different Z-ranges in one dataset
statement:
As a bioimaging data repository developer,
I want to represent fluorescence and bright-field images acquired over different Z-ranges within a single OME-Zarr dataset while preserving their spatial alignment,
so that users can visualize and analyze both images together without treating them as separate datasets.

Background and current limitations: in the dataset, fluorescence images were acquired across Z-planes 0-50, while bright-field images were acquired only at Z-planes 22-30. OME-Zarr 0.5 does not provide a standardized way to represent these images with different Z-ranges as a single spatially aligned dataset.

Possible solutions: this use case can be addressed using Scenes in OME-Zarr 0.6, which allow images with different dimensions to be grouped while preserving their spatial relationships.
workaround: Scenes (RFC-5)

title: Link segmentations to their source channels
statement: As a bioimage or medical image analyst,\nI want to store several segmentations of the same image (including overlapping ones and ones tied to specific image channels) together with my OME-Zarr image, and record what each one is and which channel it comes from,\nso that overlapping structures (e.g. nucleus and cell, organ and tumor) and channel-specific segmentations are kept without loss, and other people and tools can tell which segmentation belongs to which channel without guessing from names.

title: Multiscale levels in different storages
statement: As a data provider hosting large images,\nI want the resolution levels of an image to be able to sit in different filesets or locations (e.g. full resolution in archive storage, smaller levels on a fast server),\nso that viewers can load previews quickly, and I can add or move resolution levels without copying or rewriting the whole image.

title: Segmentations stored separately from the image
statement:
As a bioimage analyst working with public images,
I want to save my segmentations in my own fileset and link them to the original image,
so that I can create and share labels without write access to the original data or copying large images, and viewers can show image and labels together.

Also included: the need for "viewers to overlay a source OME-Zarr and a separate annotation/labels OME-Zarr at display time" (Mandloi2309, ngff#78) and ngff#42.

title: Default color and contrast per channel
statement:
As a bioimage data producer sharing multi-channel images,
I want to save a display color and contrast limits (display range) for each channel with my data,
so that any viewer opens the image looking the way I intended, and users don’t have to adjust every channel by hand.

Note: covered by the omero transitional metadata in OME-Zarr 0.6.
workaround: omero transitional metadata

title: Channels shown by default
statement: As a user opening images with many channels (e.g. 50+ in multiplexed imaging), I want the data to say which channels are switched on when the image first opens, so that I start from a readable view instead of an overlay of every channel, and the same channels show up in every viewer.\n\nNote: covered by the omero transitional metadata in OME-Zarr 0.6.
workaround: omero transitional metadata

title: Intensity range for display controls
statement:
As a viewer developer,
I want to know the meaningful intensity range of each channel (e.g. the actual minimum and maximum pixel values), separate from the default contrast,
so that contrast sliders cover a useful range instead of the full data type range (e.g. 0–65535).

Note: covered by the omero transitional metadata in OME-Zarr 0.6.
workaround: omero transitional metadata

title: Lookup tables (colormaps)
statement: As a scientist visualizing intensity data,\nI want to say which lookup table or colormap a channel should use, and whether it’s inverted,\nso that images that depend on a specific colormap (e.g. heatmaps, inverted EM) display correctly everywhere, without relying on one server or application.

title: OME-XML sidecar file
statement:
As a data steward converting proprietary file formats to OME-Zarr,
I want a standard way to store a metadata.ome.xml file accessible from my Multiscale or Collection,
so I can preserve at least as much vendor metadata as when converting to OME-TIFF.

Note: currently doable in 0.6 with the bioformats2raw.layout transitional metadata.
workaround: bioformats2raw.layout transitional metadata

title: OME-XML metadata as standardized JSON
statement: As a maintainer of a tool that reads/writes OME-Zarr,\nI want a standard way to store the same metadata captured in a metadata.ome.xml file, but using only standardized fields in JSON (e.g. in zarr.json),\nso I can preserve the vendor metadata without needing to know how to write/read/validate OME-XML and XML in general.

title: Photobleaching (FRAP) metadata
statement: As a bioimage analyst doing FRAP microscopy,\nI want to record the metadata for when the bleaching of the signal at a particular time with a lightsource. The properties of the photobleaching pulse (at least when and where it occurs) are relevant bits of metadata for this application. So I can seamlessly process the data in standardized workflows.

title: Basic axis names, units and scales
statement: 1. Microscope interfacing software reads data from microscope and writes in ome-zarr format. Axis names and units are hard coded while the scales are set based on the imaging parameters.\n2. User loads data in ImageJ/Neuroglancer and sees correct axis names and scale bars.
workaround: Feasible since 0.4 (axes + scale)

title: Prediction on a cutout aligned to the full volume
statement: 1. User runs CNN on cutout from existing volume in ome-zarr format and writes result as a new OME-Zarr volume, using a translation transformation to indicate the cutout location.\n2. User loads CNN output and original volume in ImageJ/Neuroglancer and sees output correctly aligned to original full-size volume.
workaround: Feasible since 0.4 (translation)

title: Affine registration between two volumes
statement: 1. User runs affine registration between existing volumes A and B in ome-zarr format. After computing affine transform, software modifies metadata of volume B in place to indicate the affine transform.\n2. User loads data volumes A and B in Neuroglancer and sees them correctly aligned.

title: Non-rigid registration stored as a displacement field
statement: 1. User performs non-rigid registration between existing volumes A (a canonical atlas) and B in ome-zarr format. BigWarp updates transformation meta-data in volume B, the non-rigid transformation is stored as a displacement field in ome-zarr format.\n2. User loads data volumes A and B in BigDataViewer and sees them correctly aligned.\n3. User overlays segmentations performed on original volume B (Story 2) and sees them correctly aligned.

title: Registration of slices into a volume
statement: 1. User collects multiple overlapping/non-overlapping slices and stores each in ome-zarr format with appropriate transformations.\n2. User collates all slices into a single ome-zarr volume (registering neighboring slices, joining the data, or introducing zeros/nans as necessary)\n3. [Potential] User may want to simply save the transformations necessary to create the single volume on the fly.

title: Stitching overlapping tiles
statement: Related to story 5\n1. User collects multiple overlapping 2d / 3d image tiles that are subsets of a whole.\n2. User performs stitching (e.g., with BigStitcher), and needs to track transforms from all tile spaces to world space.

title: Lens correction applied to every 2D slice
statement: 1. User working with an imaging system estimates its lens distortion as a non-linear 2D transform and stores it with NGFF.\n2. User collects a 3D image.\n3. User applies the same lens correction transform to all 2d slices of the 3D image.

title: Multiscale pyramids in a shared physical space
statement:
1. User has a large image stored at high resolution.
2. User generates a multiscale pyramid by repeatedly downsampling and storing relevant metadata.
3. User opens the pyramid with a viewer that can interpret scales correctly, on-the-fly loading works properly.
   a. User can open two individual scales and can view them in the same physical space.

title: Thickness of 2D slices
statement:
1. User collects 2d data with known / specified physical thickness.
2. User displays 2d slices in 3d with thickness displayed correctly.

Needs ability to apply M-dim transforms to N-dim data (M>N).

title: Specialized metadata for different applications
statement: 1. User collects two datasets for ML training.\n2. Each has distinct coordinateTransform for display purposes (e.g. scale [4,4,3.8], scale [4,4,4.1])\n3. They share a coordinateTransform (e.g. scale [4,4,4]) to avoid interpolation when passing data to model.

title: Reordering z-slices
statement: 1. User collects 2d images but they are written in an unpredictable order.\n2. After the fact, user writes the correct order of z-slices to transform metadata.\n3. A transformed view of the volume should display the slices in the correct order.

title: Stacking 2D images into a 3D image
statement: 1. User collects N 2d images each stored as its own array.\n2. User writes metadata to "stack" the 2d images along a third dimension using coordinateTransformations and a new coordinateSystem.\n3. Downstream software makes available a 3d image consisting of the N 2d images.

title: Thin-plate spline transformations
statement: Similar to Story 4, but the thin-plate-spline parameters are stored in ome-zarr instead of the displacement field. That should save storage space and allow for transformations of annotations that are connected to the image but don't align to the voxel grid.
workaround: Displacement field (Story 4); RFC-5 author suggested waiting for a later revision, as it depends on storing points (landmarks)

title: Mesh-affine transformations
statement: Extends story 5 and 6. A section tile is divided in a triangle-mesh (i.e. non-overlapping triangles) and each triangle gets an affine transformation attached.\n\n(axtimwalde: storing the affines is not necessary; source and target coordinates of all vertices plus three vertex indices per triangle are enough and much more compact.)
workaround: RFC-5 author suggested waiting for a later revision, as it depends on storing points (mesh)

title: Oblique plane microscopy: on-the-fly deskew
statement: 1. User collects skewed planes (OPM Snouty, Zeiss LLS7, diSPIM)\n2. Downstream software (BigDataViewer for instance) uses the skew transformation information (3d matrix for instance) to display the dataset in real physical space, without rasterisation of the dataset on an orthogonal XYZ array.

title: Stitching multi-angle acquisitions
statement:
Related to story 5 and 6
1. User collects multiple overlapping 2d / 3d image tiles that are subsets of a whole.
2. User repeats the operation 1. after having rotated significantly the sample (30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, etc.)
3. User performs stitching (e.g., with BigStitcher), and needs to track transforms from all tile and all angle spaces to world space.

title: Registering multi-position acquisitions
statement:
1. User collects 3D volumes in multiple channels at multiple positions in a 96-well plate.
2. User analyzes the volumes to register the volumes in XYZ such that the focal plane is in the center of the volume.
3. User stores separate affine transformations for all positions.
4. User would like to view registered volume in napari/neuroglancer/ImageJ.

title: Correspondence of histology to MRI coordinates
statement:
Related to 4, 5, 12 and 15, with details from the existing wb_view implementation
1. User collects T1w and other MRI scans of an animal, rigid aligns them and orients via ACPC or similar (not nonlinear or anisotropic affine)
2. Brain is extracted and sectioned, regularly spaced sections (whole brain, ~0.5mm in macaque) are stained, 2D scanned (and stitched) with full coverage (high resolution, image pyramids), with hemispheres and temporal pole pieces as separate images (due to FoV limits, separated tissue not being placed in correct relative position on the slide, bent corpus callosum misaligning hemispheres, etc)
3. Histology images are registered to MRI reference space, with the transform split into distinct parts.
   a. 2D to 2D affine for each piece to roughly position it within the section plane (for display without applying a deformation to image data)
   b. 2D to 2D deformation field (and its inverse) for each section to get accurate correspondence of histology tissue to the MRI tissue intersecting the section plane (tissue pliability, tearing, etc)
   c. 2D to 3D transform for each section to define the section plane in MRI mm space (currently affine, might include curvature in the future to deal with tissue deformation before sectioning)
4. For each image, a "distance beyond tissue edge" measurement is created for the tissue that the image is "responsible for", stored in rough aligned section plane space, used to resolve overlaps with background and/or clipped tissue when displaying all images from a section together.
5. User wants to display the histology image data one section at a time (all pieces in the section shown as per rough alignment), next to MRI data, and clicking on the histology moves the MRI display to the corresponding coordinate (and vice versa).

title: Drift correction: one transform per timepoint
statement:
Motivates transformations that transform spatial coordinates (affine etc.) but depend on / differ for non-spatial coordinates (e.g. t and c)
1. User has a timelapse of a drifting sample.
2. User performs drift correction, obtaining one (linear) transformation per timepoint.
3. User wants to save / visualize the drift corrected timelapse without resampling / transforming the timelapse.
workaround: Resample data; RFC-5 lists by-coordinate transforms as future possibility

title: Registration / stitching / multi-view reconstruction of timelapses
statement: 1. User story fits into stories 5, 6, 16, 17.\n2. Typically, resulting registration parameters vary over time (e.g. because of stage positioning errors among others)\n3. User wants to save / visualize the registered / reconstructed image dataset without resampling / transforming the timelapse.
workaround: Resample data; RFC-5 lists by-coordinate transforms as future possibility
related: STORY-028; STORY-029; STORY-039; STORY-040; STORY-042; STORY-011

title: Chromatic correction: one transform per channel
statement: 1. User has an image dataset exhibiting chromatic misalignment.\n2. User performs chromatic correction obtaining one transformation per channel.\n3. User wants to save / visualize the channel aligned image without resampling / transforming the image.
workaround: Resample data; RFC-5 lists by-coordinate transforms as future possibility

title: Registration of multiplexed imaging rounds
statement:
Goal: creating multi-channel (3d or 2d) image from multiple rounds of staining/acquisition
1. Acquire multiple rounds of 3-channel images with various markers, e.g.
   a. first round: markers A, B, C.
   b. second round: markers A, D, E.
   c. third round: markers A, F, G.
2. Register a, b and c via the common marker (A, A', A''), with elastic/non-linear or linear transformation as needed.
3. Display/process the image as 7-channel image (CZYX) with channels A, B, C, D, E, F, G without re-saving the transformed pixel/voxel data.

title: Stitching and registration of tiled, multiplexed imaging
statement:
Combination of Story 6 and Story 22
1. Collect multiple overlapping 2d / 3d image tiles that are subsets of a whole, with multiple rounds of imaging. Each round contains a common registration marker.
2. Align tiles within each round of imaging (stitching) as well as between rounds (registration) using a tool such as Ashlar. Only corrected tile transformations are stored.
3. Display/process combined image with all tiles and all channels without re-saving the original image data.

(This also requires illumination/shading correction to be applied in step 3, but this correction is an intensity transform rather than a spatial coordinate transform so is not really in scope here.)

title: Cropping: bounds on an axis
statement: Motivates bounded (projective) coordinate spaces; intended for a follow-up transform RFC, not expected to be implemented in RFC-5\n1. User generates an N-D image.\n2. User defines a lower and upper bound to an axis.
workaround: Not in RFC-5; intended for a follow-up transform RFC

title: Kymographs
statement:
Motivates bounded (projective) coordinate spaces; intended for a follow-up transform RFC, not expected to be implemented in RFC-5
1. User has 2D+time data.
2. User defines a line in 2D space.
3. Displays/process to a 2D image of time-line coordinate space.
workaround: Not in RFC-5; intended for a follow-up transform RFC

title: Curvilinear tube projection
statement:
Motivates bounded (projective) coordinate spaces; intended for a follow-up transform RFC, not expected to be implemented in RFC-5
1. User generates 3D + channel data.
2. User defines a spline in 3D space.
3. Process to an axis-aligned bounded space transformed around the spline.
workaround: Not in RFC-5; intended for a follow-up transform RFC

title: Mesh projection / surface quantification
statement:
Motivates bounded (projective) coordinate spaces; intended for a follow-up transform RFC, not expected to be implemented in RFC-5
1. User has a 3D image.
2. User defines a 2D surface mesh in 3D space.
3. User gets image values at the mesh coordinates / projected to the mesh coordinates.
workaround: Not in RFC-5; intended for a follow-up transform RFC

title: CMI experiment as a graph of warped datasets
statement:
A correlative multimodal imaging experiment often involves multiple (>2) 3D datasets. A graph can be built such as: datasets are nodes; warp functions between any two datasets are edges linking these two nodes. A warp function (edge) between any two datasets can be defined by a set of parameters defining the origin and target datasets (e.g. dataset name, voxel size in metric units, offset, scale, axis flips) and a list of the coordinates of paired landmarks between these datasets. In this way, all edges and nodes can be listed in tables. The list of landmarks and warp functions can be sourced from BigWarp (and stored alongside the warp graph). This approach allows combining multiple warps in sequence (warping data across connected nodes in the graph). This approach not only allows warping the datasets themselves, but also the annotations drawn on any dataset. Any feature drawn on any dataset can be then overlaid onto any of the connected datasets seamlessly. Advantages:
1. Version control: the warp graph can be managed through git.
2. Scalability: more complex CMI workflows can be robustly built and shared efficiently across collaborators, e.g. a correlative light - XRay - EM workflow with multiple X-ray CT datasets obtained at different trimming stages.
3. Accuracy: by warping the annotations, any analysis can take place in the originally acquired datasets (instead of segmenting the warped datasets, which may have incorporated interpolation noise)
4. Cost-efficiency: packaging a CMI experiment only requires a single version of the original datasets (data-heavy) and the warp table (data-light); no dataset duplicates are needed.

This system has already been incorporated into an NGFF OME-Zarr data ecosystem (WEBKNOSSOS) as warpAnnotations, which facilitates multiuser collaboration and releasing CMI experiments.

title: Annotating and training with reference crops
statement:
1. User runs annotation tools (e.g. micro-sam) to segment reference crops (one or multiple); a reference crop is the same as the cut-outs in previous stories.
2. User writes the resulting annotated reference crop(s) in a new OME-Zarr volume (following Story 2).
   a. An interesting use-case would be to do the above two steps for data on an OMERO server (and ensure that the user does not have to create a zero array locally to do step 2)
3. User wants to train models on segmented reference crops only.
